opus-5.5.text:
I think the optimizer work is a good example because, at the beginning, almost nobody believed it was worth doing. For close to ten years, Adam and its variants like AdamW have been the default. Most people treat the optimizer as solved and assume the real gains come from data, architecture, or scale. So if you say you want to replace Adam in large-scale pretraining, the usual reaction is skepticism. People have tried for years, many papers claim improvements on small models, and almost none of them hold up at scale.

When we looked at Muon, there were promising signals at small scale, but there were also real problems. As we scaled up, we hit training instabilities. For example, the attention logits could blow up. So it wasn't a case of taking something off the shelf and having it work. We had to understand why it broke and fix it properly. That's where things like weight decay adjustments and, later, the QK-clip technique came from. We spent a lot of effort making it stable for a model at the trillion-parameter scale.

I'd say it's a successful non-consensus bet for three reasons.

First, the payoff is fundamental. If an optimizer gives you meaningfully better token efficiency, that's very valuable, because high-quality data is becoming a bottleneck. Getting more intelligence out of each token matters more and more. So it's not a marginal trick. It changes the efficiency of the whole pretraining process.

Second, we didn't just believe in it. We verified it carefully. Non-consensus doesn't mean being contrarian for its own sake. You need a good reason to think everyone else might be wrong, and then you need very rigorous experiments: scaling-law comparisons, controlled ablations, checking whether the advantage persists as you scale up instead of disappearing. Only after that did we commit to using it for a real flagship model.

Third, we actually put it into production. Many ideas stay at the paper level. We trained a large model with it end to end and showed that you can get a smooth loss curve without loss spikes. That's when it stops being an interesting idea and becomes a technical capability.

More broadly, I think this reflects how a team like ours has to operate. If you just follow consensus, you're competing on resources with much bigger players, and you'll usually lose. Your real advantage has to come from a few places where you see something others don't, and where you're willing to put in the effort to make it work. The optimizer was one of those places. Of course, not every non-consensus bet pays off. But you need the taste to choose the right ones and the persistence to push through the stage where it doesn't work yet.

r001.rationale: The response says Adam and its variants had been the default and describes the team's goal as replacing Adam with Muon.

r002.rationale: It attributes the optimizer's fundamental payoff to meaningfully better token efficiency, saying it gets more intelligence out of each token.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the Muon story is a good example because, at the time we started, the consensus was very clear: AdamW is the optimizer. Everybody used it, every big model was trained with it, and if you proposed something else, the default reaction was that it must have a hidden flaw, otherwise somebody would have done it already. Muon existed as an idea in the community, but it was mostly demonstrated on small-scale experiments, things like speedrun benchmarks. The common belief was that these tricks don't transfer when you scale up. We've all seen many optimizers that look great at 100 million parameters and then fall apart at a few billion.

So the non-consensus part wasn't inventing the idea from scratch. It was deciding to actually bet on it and do the engineering to make it work at scale, when most people thought that was a waste of time. We had to solve some very concrete problems. For example, the original formulation didn't have weight decay, and without that, at large scale the weights grow and training becomes unstable. We also had to figure out how to match the update scale across different matrix shapes so that you could reuse the hyperparameters people already know from AdamW, instead of retuning everything. Those sound like small details, but they are the difference between a toy result and something you can put into a real pretraining run.

What made it a success in my view is that the result was measurable and reproducible. We saw roughly a two times improvement in compute efficiency compared to AdamW on scaling law experiments, and then we validated it on a real model with a three billion active and sixteen billion total parameters mixture of experts. It wasn't just a paper claim. The same optimizer later went into Kimi K2, a trillion-parameter model, and the training was stable for the whole run. That's the real test. An optimizer that works at that scale is no longer a research curiosity.

I also think the way it happened says something about how to do this kind of work. You need a small team with conviction, you need to be willing to spend real compute on something that might fail, and you need a rigorous way to tell whether you're actually winning rather than fooling yourself. A lot of non-consensus ideas fail not because they're wrong but because the people pursuing them never build the infrastructure to prove they're right. Scaling laws are that infrastructure. If you can show the curve shifts consistently across several orders of magnitude, you can convince yourself and others, and that's when the consensus starts to move.

r001.rationale: It says AdamW was the prevailing optimizer and that the team chose to bet on Muon instead.

r002.rationale: It reports roughly a twofold compute-efficiency improvement over AdamW in scaling-law experiments, conveying a substantial efficiency gain.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that we treated the optimizer as something worth questioning, even when using an established optimizer was the obvious choice. That’s a difficult research bet, because you have to invest effort before you know whether the gains will justify it.

But being non-consensus isn’t itself a success. You need evidence that the alternative actually works better under the constraints you care about. For an optimizer, that means asking whether it helps you reach the same model quality with less compute, and whether the improvement holds as you scale.

So, to me, the successful part is turning an unconventional hypothesis into a practical advantage. The lesson isn’t to disagree with everyone; it’s to identify an assumption worth testing and be willing to do the work to test it.

r002.rationale: It mentions reaching the same model quality with less compute, but does not communicate a substantial improvement in token efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that we questioned something most people treated as settled. With an optimizer, the conventional view is often: use what already works and put your effort into scaling the model. Spending time on a different approach can look like an unnecessary risk.

But being non-consensus isn’t valuable by itself. You need a technical hypothesis, experiments that can disprove it, and evidence that the improvement survives at scale. To me, that’s what makes this kind of work successful: turning an unconventional idea into a practical advantage, rather than simply having a different opinion.

r001.rationale: It describes challenging a conventional approach generally, but never identifies Adam or says the optimizer departed from its use.

r002.rationale: It mentions practical advantage and improvement at scale, but does not attribute success to improved token efficiency.
